with_skill.expectation: Runs an interview before producing the register, asking one question at a time.
Builds the register by working through a named risk taxonomy rather than brainstorming risks from a blank page.

Anchors impact against non-recoverable committed spend and reputational loss rather than schedule slip, and states that an event's date does not move so schedule risk collapses into a binary go/no-go.
Register rows carry a named owner and a review date, not just a score.
States explicitly that general liability does not cover cancellation, lost revenue, or any of the organizer's own financial loss.
States that insurers excluded the communicable-disease peril market-wide from late January 2020, and that it has been available since only as a specifically negotiated endorsement.
Warns that a trigger that never fires in a bad year is worse than no cover, because it was still paid for.
States that general liability frequently does not pay attendee medical expenses, which is why participant accident cover complements rather than duplicates it.
Produces the emergency plan as a document separate from the risk register, and says why - it is read under pressure by people, including volunteers, who never saw the register.

Does not rank or prioritise the named scenarios against each other, and states their ordering is set by the venue's own construction, the format and local emergency-services protocol rather than any value-per-effort calculation.
Declines to state whether this clause returns the deposit, and routes the actual clause to counsel.
Says force-majeure protection is only as good as the specific words negotiated in advance, and that the phrase "force majeure" alone settles nothing.
Says frustration-of-purpose arguments rarely rescue an organizer where the contract already allocated the risk or contains explicit no-refund language.
Recommends reviewing and updating the named event list as new foreseeable risks emerge, rather than treating it as boilerplate.
Does not assert that the 30k EUR deposit is or is not recoverable.
States that likelihood and impact are time-phased, and that a speaker dropout six weeks out is a different risk from the same dropout six months out.
Works the treatment menu for the residual risk - prevention, contingency, impact reduction, transfer, documented acceptance - rather than jumping straight to one action.
States that the default treatment is prevention, and names the condition that promotes a risk to transfer: residual impact after prevention still exceeding what the organizing entity could absorb.
Explains that non-appearance cover indemnifies revenue and expenses when the event is cancelled or curtailed because of the named individual, not the cost of substituting a speaker.
Promotes the coverage rungs that bind or resolve fast, because of the 10-week hard date.
Compresses register depth rather than recommending deep per-risk treatment, citing the roughly 6 hours a week effort ceiling.
Promotes the durable options - a reusable register and a standing review cadence - because the company runs roughly six of these events a year.
States that a ruled-out option left at the bottom of a list silently reappears as scope later.
Says a named-risk list cannot order the work, which is the only question the register exists to answer.
Notes that poor ticket sales or lack of interest is a standard exclusion in event cancellation cover, so insurance does not rescue this scenario.
Names organizer discretion - the organizing group deciding not to run the edition with no external trigger - as a legitimate, documented outcome of this call rather than a failure.

without_skill.expectation: States, before any register content or interview question, that this is not legal or insurance advice.
Routes contract and clause wording (force majeure, cancellation, refund, indemnity) to counsel, and policy wording, limits and exclusions to a licensed broker.
Runs an interview before producing the register, asking one question at a time.
Asks whether the venue contract carries a cancellation-fee schedule and requests its step-up dates and percentages verbatim.
Asks or establishes whether the event is community-run or company-run, and treats Kestrel Data as the company-run pole.
Builds the register by working through a named risk taxonomy rather than brainstorming risks from a blank page.
Register includes organizer financial or payment-processing capability (cannot legally invoice, collect or hold money in time) as its own row.
Register includes structural or commercial defection - exhibitors or sponsors abandoning the format for their own channels - as its own row, distinct from demand shortfall.
Register includes organizer discretion, the organizing group itself deciding not to run the edition with no external trigger, as its own row.
Scores each risk on a 5x5 likelihood x impact matrix producing a score in the 1-25 range.

Anchors impact against non-recoverable committed spend and reputational loss rather than schedule slip, and states that an event's date does not move so schedule risk collapses into a binary go/no-go.
Uses four escalation bands at the boundaries Green 1-4, Yellow 5-9, Orange 10-15, Red 16-25.
Register rows carry a named owner and a review date, not just a score.
States that this is not legal or insurance advice before giving any coverage recommendation.
Identifies the event as the community-run pole and says the recommendation assumes that pole.
Says a cancellation policy protects nothing here because there is no non-recoverable committed spend to protect.
States explicitly that general liability does not cover cancellation, lost revenue, or any of the organizer's own financial loss.
Names key-organizer loss - the one person holding a critical function becoming unavailable - as a risk that actually bites at this pole.
Frames the main exposure at this pole as organizational rather than financial.
States it is not legal advice and routes the clause itself to counsel.
Treats the 85% pickup requirement on 240 room nights as a second, parallel financial cliff on its own schedule, separate from the cancellation-fee curve.
Recommends the polled go/no-go format in which each area owner votes go or no-go and a single no-go halts the sequence.
Names the areas to poll, including registration or ticket pace against break-even, room-block pickup against the attrition threshold, and contractual exposure (which deadlines have already passed).
States that cancelling earlier at a lower step-up can beat waiting for a force-majeure or legal outcome that is never guaranteed.
States it is not insurance advice and that whether any policy responds to a specific loss is a question for the broker reading the actual wording.
Recommends asking explicitly whether the cancellation form includes a communicable-disease buy-back, and what it costs.
States that insurers excluded the communicable-disease peril market-wide from late January 2020, and that it has been available since only as a specifically negotiated endorsement.
Instructs recording the disease buy-back decision either way, with its reason, including when it is declined.
For any parametric structure, says to ask which station measures the index, over which hours, and what the trigger would have paid in prior years.
Warns that a trigger that never fires in a bad year is worse than no cover, because it was still paid for.
Recommends participant accident cover and ties it to the hands-on hardware (soldering bench, drone cage) rather than offering it generically.
States that general liability frequently does not pay attendee medical expenses, which is why participant accident cover complements rather than duplicates it.
Recommends the event cancellation rung and ties the recommendation to non-recoverable committed spend as a share of the total budget.
Names standard event cancellation exclusions that matter here, including voluntary cancellation and poor ticket sales or lack of interest.
Labels any carrier, premium band or limit mentioned as an illustrative example of a coverage category rather than a quote, a recommendation, or a claim of availability in this jurisdiction.
Produces the emergency plan as a document separate from the risk register, and says why - it is read under pressure by people, including volunteers, who never saw the register.
Covers theft of equipment, naming attendee laptops and event networking or AV gear.
Covers evacuation for any other reason, including who confirms the building is clear.

Does not rank or prioritise the named scenarios against each other, and states their ordering is set by the venue's own construction, the format and local emergency-services protocol rather than any value-per-effort calculation.

Requires a physical printed copy on site, and says a plan living only in a shared drive fails at exactly the moment power loss, connectivity loss, dead phones or evacuation are what triggered the need for it.
Lists the non-emergency police line, explicitly labelled as distinct from the emergency number.
Lists each lead organizer with the specific hours they will be on-site and reachable, not just a name and a number.
Recommends notifying local emergency services in advance that a large event with many non-local attendees is running.
Declines to state whether this clause returns the deposit, and routes the actual clause to counsel.
Does not draft replacement or additional clause language.

States that a clause expressly saying the venue shall refund all payments produced a full deposit refund in one court outcome, while a near-identical fact pattern with a clause silent on deposits denied one.
Says force-majeure protection is only as good as the specific words negotiated in advance, and that the phrase "force majeure" alone settles nothing.

Explains that because epidemics, terrorism, labour disputes and hazardous weather are now foreseeable, they must be named in the contract, or a court may find the organizer accepted the risk by not naming them.
Says frustration-of-purpose arguments rarely rescue an organizer where the contract already allocated the risk or contains explicit no-refund language.
Recommends reviewing and updating the named event list as new foreseeable risks emerge, rather than treating it as boilerplate.
Does not assert that the 30k EUR deposit is or is not recoverable.
Re-scores the relevant register rows at today's distance from the event rather than reusing scores set when the register was written.
States that likelihood and impact are time-phased, and that a speaker dropout six weeks out is a different risk from the same dropout six months out.
Works the treatment menu for the residual risk - prevention, contingency, impact reduction, transfer, documented acceptance - rather than jumping straight to one action.
States that the default treatment is prevention, and names the condition that promotes a risk to transfer: residual impact after prevention still exceeding what the organizing entity could absorb.
States that non-appearance cover typically must be bound at least 14 days before the event, and cannot be bound now for this edition after the loss.
Says non-appearance cover is only worth buying where a single named person genuinely carries the event's value, and that a balanced multi-track program is not exposed this way.
Flags single-source dependency - one keynote the program was built around - as an amplifier raising the scored impact of this row.
Records the coverage decision and its reason for the next edition rather than treating the question as closed once this edition is handled.
Treats refund exposure and attendee communication as scored impact-reduction steps inside the register rather than as the whole answer.
Does not claim that a specific policy would or would not have paid for this loss.
States that this is not insurance advice and routes the "would it have paid" question to a licensed broker.
Measures surprise rate - risks that materialised with no corresponding register row - as a named metric.
Maps the unpaid 12k EUR sponsor invoice to a sponsor-withdrawal row covering a signed sponsor that never pays.
Maps the ticketing-platform outage to a registration-platform breach, data-loss or outage row.
Measures owner and review-date coverage - the share of rows carrying both - and states that a row with neither is a note, not a managed risk.
Measures decision-date discipline: whether every internal go/no-go date landed before its contractual fee step-up, and whether each was held rather than skipped.
Measures re-score freshness: whether scores were actually revisited at each decision date.
Measures coverage-decision traceability: whether each declined coverage rung has a recorded reason, findable after the fact.
Identifies "opened it twice" as the core failure and binds the re-score to the decision dates so it happens whether or not anyone remembers.
States that any pass thresholds it offers are defaults this guidance sets rather than an event-industry benchmark, and invites the team to set its own bar.
Recommends a post-event closing pass run within about a week of doors closing, recording which risks materialised and which of those had no register row.
Says explicitly which stated constraint moved which option in the re-ranked menus, rather than presenting a default ordering unchanged.
Notes that with no external venue contract there is no escalating cancellation-fee curve, so the decision dates must hang on the team's own committed spend and its own limit instead.
Promotes the durable options - a reusable register and a standing review cadence - because the company runs roughly six of these events a year.
Deletes options ruled out by the stated constraints from the plan rather than parking them at the bottom of a list.
States that a ruled-out option left at the bottom of a list silently reappears as scope later.
Says a named-risk list cannot order the work, which is the only question the register exists to answer.
Names whoever outside the organizing team owns the cancellation decision - the budget holder or the parent organisation - and puts them in the go/no-go call, because this is company-run.
Uses the polled format in which each area owner votes go or no-go and a single no-go halts, given the co-founders are split.
Names areas to poll beyond ticket pace, including contractual exposure, payment integrity (whether the team can actually collect and refund), and speaker and sponsor confirmation status.
Notes that poor ticket sales or lack of interest is a standard exclusion in event cancellation cover, so insurance does not rescue this scenario.
Re-scores the demand-shortfall row at today's distance from the event rather than carrying its original score.
Names organizer discretion - the organizing group deciding not to run the edition with no external trigger - as a legitimate, documented outcome of this call rather than a failure.
